body:
MUCKRAKERS AND LAWMAKERS (lesson)
Sourcing: Sinclair, a socialist novelist, wrote to expose immigrant workers' lives; Roosevelt, the president, spoke both to praise and to warn reform journalists; the amendments are constitutional law, ratified by the states. Strong answers note that a novel is fiction based on investigation, so its details need corroboration (Roosevelt's investigators confirmed many conditions).
Context: rapid urban and industrial growth, immigrant labor in the stockyards, mass-circulation magazines; growing demands for women's suffrage after decades of organizing.
Claim: strong answers argue that muckrakers created public pressure that moved government to act quickly when the public felt personally threatened (the stomach), while the amendments show reform reaching into the structure of government itself. Sinclair's own words show the reform he got (food safety) was not the one he wanted (workers' lives).
Corroboration: the 1906 laws themselves, the investigators' report to Roosevelt, sales figures for the novel, later labor laws.

THE MOST IMPORTANT PROGRESSIVE REFORM (assignment, showcase)
Any reform can earn Advanced if argued well. Strong essays: the Nineteenth Amendment (barred denying the vote on account of sex, ending sex discrimination in voting law nationwide, though many Black women in the South remained disenfranchised until 1965); the Sixteenth Amendment (made the modern federal government financially possible); consumer protection (foundation of today's food and drug regulation); antitrust (the idea that government may break up monopolies). The alternative must be treated fairly with specific evidence.

PROGRESSIVE ERA DOCUMENT CHECK (assessment)
1. Congress may tax incomes "from whatever source derived" without apportioning the tax among the states by population. It answered the Populist and Progressive demand for a graduated income tax and gave the federal government a large, steady source of revenue.
2. Senators are "elected by the people" of each state, rather than chosen by state legislatures. It answered charges that wealthy interests and party machines bought Senate seats through legislatures.
3. It bars the United States or any state from denying the vote "on account of sex." It does not guarantee the vote to every woman: poll taxes, literacy tests and violence still kept most Black women, and men, in the South from voting, and some Asian immigrant women were barred from citizenship.
4. Expected: Sinclair aimed at the public's heart (workers' suffering) but readers reacted to the danger to their own food (stomach). Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act (June 30, 1906) but not labor protections for packinghouse workers.
5. Roosevelt says exposing wrongdoing ("filth on the floor") is sometimes the most needed service; elsewhere in the speech he warns that critics who never do anything but expose wrongs can do harm. Strong answers explain that he wanted reform under his leadership, not radical attacks on the system.
6. Strong answers name a group (Black Americans in the segregated South, immigrants, workers whose child labor law was struck down in 1918) and give evidence from the reference card.

Scoring tip: on question 3 and question 6, a student who says only "women got the vote" earns Developing on Reasoning; Proficient requires naming who was still excluded and how.
title: Answer key: The Progressive Era
